title: Classify angles as acute, right, obtuse, straight or reflex

lesson.title: Naming Angles: Small, Square, Wide and Wider

steps.say: You already know how to sort shapes by looking at their corners — like telling a square apart from a stretched-out diamond. Today we give those corners their proper names, so you can say exactly how open an angle is.

visual.caption: A corner of a square: exactly 90 degrees

steps.say: Here is the whole idea. An angle is just how far one arm has swung open from the other, like a door opening. A right angle is exactly ninety degrees, the perfect square corner. Anything smaller than ninety, but bigger than zero, is called acute — think of a sharp little pizza slice.

visual.caption: Forty degrees — acute, smaller than a square corner

steps.say: Now keep swinging that door open. Past ninety but not yet flat is obtuse — a wide, lazy angle. When the arms lie in a perfectly flat line, that is a straight angle, one hundred eighty degrees. And if the door swings even further, past one hundred eighty, we call it reflex — the big outside angle.

visual.caption: One hundred thirty degrees — obtuse, wider than a square corner

steps.say: Let us try one. Imagine the ramp at the Skytrain station: the handrail meets the flat floor and opens to two hundred fifteen degrees on the outside. Compare it to our landmarks. Is two hundred fifteen more than one hundred eighty? Yes it is. Is it less than three hundred sixty, a full turn? Yes. So it sits between straight and a full circle, which makes it reflex.

visual.caption: Two hundred fifteen degrees — reflex, past the flat line

steps.say: Here is the trap I want you to dodge. Lots of kids look at two angles and pick the one with the longer arms as the bigger angle. That is not how it works! If I draw a thirty degree angle with arms one centimetre long, and another thirty degree angle with arms ten centimetres long, both are still thirty degrees. Both are acute. Stretching the arms is like opening a door wider by buying a longer door — the doorway opening never changed. Only the spread between the arms counts.

visual.caption: Thirty degrees — long arms or short arms, the opening is the same

steps.say: So remember: measure the opening, not the arms. Under ninety is acute, exactly ninety is right, between ninety and one eighty is obtuse, exactly one eighty is straight, and over one eighty is reflex.

lesson.answer: An angle's name comes from how far open it is, never from how long its arms are: under 90 is acute, 90 is right, 90 to 180 is obtuse, 180 is straight, over 180 is reflex.

practice.question: At the Vancouver ferry dock, a loading ramp is lowered so the angle between the ramp and the flat deck measures one hundred five degrees. Draw that angle if it helps. What kind of angle is it — acute, right, obtuse, straight, or reflex? Then, if a friend says a different ramp must have a bigger angle just because its arms are three metres long instead of one metre, is your friend right?
practice.answer: One hundred five degrees is obtuse, because it is more than ninety but less than one hundred eighty. And no, the friend is wrong — arm length has nothing to do with angle size; only how far the arms are opened apart matters.
